_source: brain-authored narrative for the sample-run fixture (GLM-5.3-Flash, 16x H100, chatbot)
title: Serving GLM-5.3-Flash on sixteen H100s
standfirst: A configuration search over three serving shapes and 27 simulated runs on the blis-latency-kernel backend, and what they say about how to run this model on 16 H100s while holding every user above 50 tok/s.
meta: Interactivity floor 50 tok/s/user (ITL p99 ≤ 20 ms), headroom 0.8

hero.html: Three topologies within 16 H100s — tensor-parallel 8 as one or two instances, and TP4 as four — each probed up the concurrency axis and bisected to its interactivity limit. 27 runs in all; 17 met every service limit (checked per instance, not just the cluster average), 10 did not and are reported rather than dropped.

The kernel shows a sharp interactivity cliff for this model: per-user token rate holds flat, then collapses within one or two sessions of a configuration's limit. The limit — not the peak throughput — is what separates the three shapes.

Four TP4 instances with expert parallel, at a usable operating point of 16 concurrent sessions. It delivers 1,264 tok/s across the fleet (79 tok/s per GPU) while every user still sees ~74 tok/s, and it scales furthest before the cliff.

explore_prose: Everything below comes from these 27 runs: each is one of three configurations at one concurrency level, priced on the blis-latency-kernel backend.

Click any value to filter. The counts, the scatter and the table update together — filter to the servable runs, or to a single topology, and the figures in the sections below can be checked against the raw rows here.

sections.title: The operating curve, and where it stops
prose: Every configuration trades the same way while it is healthy: serve more sessions, the fleet delivers more tokens, each user waits a little longer. Then the inter-token latency crosses its ceiling and the per-user rate falls off a cliff — the hollow markers.

The single-instance TP8 shape reaches only 6 concurrent sessions before the cliff; two TP8 instances reach 12; four TP4 instances reach 20. Capacity is set by how many instances share the load, not by any single engine knob.

The recommendation reads the usable point at headroom 0.8 of each limit, not the edge: 4× TP4 + EP at 16 sessions, where it holds ~74 tok/s per user and 1,264 tok/s across the fleet. (C* is 20, not the apparent 25: at 24-25 sessions the cluster-average ITL still looks fine, but one of the four instances is already over the 20 ms ceiling.)
sections.caption_note: The dashed line is this run's 50 tok/s/user floor; the y axis is the per-user token rate on a p99 basis.

sections.title: How far each configuration scales
prose: The same three configurations, reduced to one number each: the highest concurrency that stays inside every service limit — measured per instance, not on the cluster average. The spread is 6 to 20 sessions — more than a factor of three from configuration alone, on 16 H100s and one fixed workload.

The cross marks the first load that breaks a limit. On this model every break is the same one: inter-token latency crossing the 20 ms p99 ceiling. There are no KV preemptions in any run — the cliff is a decode-compute ceiling, not a memory one.
sections.caption_note: Here that is a four-fold spread in capacity from configuration alone — same 16 H100s, same chatbot workload.

sections.title: Why the fastest-looking configuration can be the wrong one
prose: Ranking configurations on peak fleet throughput alone would promote the runs on the right of Figure 1 — the ones past their cliff. The tail latency is the independent check: those same runs sit low and to the right here, slow per user and slow at the tail at once.
This is why the search ranks on usable capacity at the interactivity floor, not on the highest fleet number any run produced.
sections.caption_note: On this run the two move together, so the tail corroborates the per-user story rather than contradicting it.

recommendation_prose: Run four TP4 instances with expert parallel. On this workload it serves the most sessions before the interactivity cliff and wins on both the budget-max and per-GPU axes.
These are simulator predictions from the kernel backend — spot-check the flat ITL and the cliff location against the real llm-d measurements before acting.

glossary.def: The output tokens per second one caller sees, computed as 1000 divided by the p99 inter-token latency.
glossary.long: The interactivity axis of the search, on the same p99 basis as the floor: 50 tok/s/user is an ITL p99 at or below 20 ms.

glossary.def: The average gap between consecutive output tokens in a response.
glossary.long: On this model the kernel prices it as nearly flat until a decode-compute ceiling, then it climbs sharply — the cliff in Figure 1.

glossary.def: How many GPUs each copy of the model is split across.
glossary.long: Written into the generated scenario as parallel.tp. TP8 fills one H100 node; TP4 lets four instances share the 16-GPU budget.
